items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: Year-end reflection essay "2025" (LinkedIn/X)
items.quote: At the same time, it appears likely the Fed will be inclined to ease to push real interest rates down.
items.summary: Dalio says the Fed and the incoming chair will likely be biased to push nominal and real rates down, which supports asset prices and inflates bubbles, though he doubts easing will be as large as priced. With nearly $10tn of debt to roll, he finds long bonds unappealing and expects a steeper curve. He calls the AI boom an early-stage bubble.
items.score_note: Expects an easing bias from the new chair/FOMC, but says easing may be less than the market discounts; so -1 rather than -2.
items.ai_quote: obviously the AI boom that is now in the early stages of a bubble had a big effect on everything

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: Bloomberg TV, The David Rubenstein Show (aired Jan 8; quotes via Fortune/Yahoo write-up of Jan 9)
items.quote: They print money, devalue the currency, and create an artificially low interest rate
items.summary: On the $38 trillion national debt, Dalio says countries that essentially go broke always print money, devalue the currency and hold interest rates artificially low, hurting bondholders. He says future generations will repay the debt in devalued dollars and recommends TIPS and 10-15% gold.
items.score_note: Left unscored: a long-run debt-monetization thesis (governments print money and hold rates artificially low), not a view on the Fed's policy-rate path at this time. Sub-collector had proposed -1 forecast. Describes the historical playbook (print, devalue, artificially low rates) as what will happen; a structural forecast, not a call on the next meeting.

items.speaker: Bill Ackman
items.occasion: X post (later deleted) replying to Trump's call for a one-year 10% cap on credit card interest rates, plus follow-up post
items.quote: The best way to bring down rates would be to make it more competitive by making the regulatory regime more conducive to new entrants and new technologies.
items.summary: Ackman called Trump's proposed 10% credit-card rate cap a mistake, saying lenders unable to price for losses would cancel cards for millions and push them to loan sharks. He said the goal of lower card rates is worthy but should be reached through more competition and lighter regulation for new entrants.
items.score_note: No view on the Fed policy rate; about a consumer credit price cap and credit availability.

items.speaker: Bill Ackman
items.occasion: X post to Trump, Bessent and FHFA's Pulte proposing prepayment penalties on new Fannie/Freddie mortgages to lower mortgage rates
items.quote: One of the unique features of U.S. conventional mortgages is that they are prepayable at any time without a penalty,
items.summary: Ackman argued that the free prepayment option forces MBS buyers to demand a wider spread, and that offering mortgages with prepayment penalties could cut mortgage rates by roughly 65 basis points. He asked the administration to have Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac offer such loans.
items.score_note: Mortgage-spread structure proposal, not a view on the Fed policy-rate path.

items.speaker: Bill Ackman
items.occasion: Fireside chat with UBS's Iqbal Khan at UBS Asia Wealth Forum 2026, Singapore (morning of Jan 12 Singapore time = evening Jan 11 US Eastern)
items.quote: I think the Fed will abandon the goal of 2%.
items.summary: Ackman said a return to 2% inflation is fiction and the Fed will end up with a 2.5%-3% goal. He doubted the couple of further Fed cuts the market expects, saying tax cuts, deregulation and heavy AI investment are driving growth that is partly inflationary, and that the Fed is not heading back to meaningfully low rates.
items.score_note: Forecast of fewer cuts than the market expects and no return to low rates (+1). A higher tolerated inflation goal is itself dovish, so kept at +1 rather than +2; he did not call for hikes.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Jan 11 edition)
items.quote: The core policy question is whether these trends remain consistent with Fed Chair Powell’s view that the central bank is "well-positioned" to remain patient on interest rates.
items.summary: Reviewing the latest labor data and looking ahead to inflation figures, El-Erian says US data show employment decoupling from strong growth. He frames the key question as whether inflation and labor trends still fit Powell's view that the Fed can stay patient on rates.
items.score_note: Frames the Fed as on a patient hold and poses an open question; no lean either way.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: LinkedIn post reacting to a New York Times report on the Fed chair (evening of Jan 11 ET)
items.quote: This is the scenario I feared months ago when I suggested the Chair step down to protect the institution’s independence.
items.summary: Commenting on a New York Times report about the Fed chair, El-Erian warns the situation could expose deeper issues and further undermine the credibility of a Fed whose public standing is already fragile. He recalls having suggested months earlier that the Chair step down to protect independence and says the nominee to replace him must be committed to the reforms needed to restore the Fed's effectiveness.
items.score_note: About Fed independence, credibility and reform; no statement on the rate path.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Project Syndicate op-ed on the 2026 outlook for the AI-led market rally, as quoted by Business Insider
items.quote: The animal spirits that drove indiscriminate, massive financing last year will increasingly be tamed by bubble fears that force investors to be more selective
items.summary: El-Erian argues the AI narrative will not be strong enough in 2026 to overshadow structural uncertainties such as a K-shaped economy and geopolitics. He says last year's indiscriminate, massive financing will be restrained by bubble fears. No view on the Fed rate path.
items.score_note: No rate-path content; statement is about AI-related financing and bubble fears.
items.ai_quote: The animal spirits that drove indiscriminate, massive financing last year will increasingly be tamed by bubble fears that force investors to be more selective

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: Media call after JPMorgan Q4 2025 results (reporters' call, not the analyst call)
items.quote: It will probably raise inflation expectations.
items.summary: Asked about the DOJ criminal inquiry into Fed Chair Powell, Dimon said he has enormous respect for Powell and that anything chipping away at Fed independence is not a good idea. He said it would have the reverse consequences of what the administration wants and probably raise inflation expectations.
items.score_note: Fed independence only; he states no view on the policy rate path, only that political pressure would backfire via inflation expectations.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
items.occasion: DoubleLine annual 'Just Markets' webcast ('Clue'); quotes via ETF Trends recap dated Jan 14
items.quote: You’re better off in cash than 30-year Treasuries,
items.summary: Gundlach said the 'weapon' hurting markets is the deficit-based economy and that the two-year Treasury will outperform the 30-year. The recap says he noted the two-year yield has stopped falling and that the Fed follows the two-year; he cited waning confidence in central bankers and inflationary policies behind gold's rise.
items.score_note: No direct quote on the policy path; the recap paraphrases that the two-year yield stopped falling and the Fed tracks it, which implies a hold. Scored 0 on that paraphrase (nearer 0 than +1).

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: US Chamber of Commerce event, conversation with David Rubenstein
items.quote: it will drive rates higher not lower
items.summary: Dimon ruled out ever being Fed chair and repeated that interfering with Fed independence would push rates up rather than down. He added that everyone he knows, including the president, says an independent Fed board is needed. Coverage of the same event also has him warning that US deficits are not sustainable.
items.score_note: Statement is about Fed independence and its effect on market rates, not about what the Fed should or will do with the policy rate.

items.speaker: Larry Fink
items.occasion: CNBC 'Squawk on the Street' interview on BlackRock Q4 2025 results day (transcript posted by BlackRock on Jan 23)
items.quote: There’s good justification for lowering rates if you believe in the productivity power of AI and the deflationary impact of China’s $1 trillion trade surplus.
items.summary: Fink expected a steeper yield curve in 2026 and said there is good justification for lowering rates because AI and China's trade surplus are deflationary. He said the US is too focused on monetary policy and not enough on fiscal discipline, and that deficits could one day produce low inflation but elevated interest rates if foreign buyers hesitate. On AI infrastructure he said he does not see a bubble and fears under-investment.
items.score_note: Says lowering rates is justified (leans easier) but conditions it on the AI-deflation thesis and warns deficits can push long rates up, so -1 rather than -2. Business Insider's same-day report of his CNBC remarks adds a non-base-case scenario of the 10-year above 5%. The BlackRock page is dated Jan 23 (posting date); the interview was on results day, Jan 15.
items.ai_quote: But we’re working with hyperscalers who are giving us 15‑ to 20‑year leases.

items.speaker: Ted Pick
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Q4 2025 earnings call (prepared remarks)
items.quote: 2026 starts with the tailwinds of constructive fiscal policy and easier monetary policy.
items.summary: Pick opens the call saying the US economy proved resilient in 2025 and that 2026 begins with constructive fiscal policy and easier monetary policy as tailwinds for capital markets, with geopolitics front and center.
items.score_note: Describes easier monetary policy as an existing tailwind; no statement on what the Fed will or should do next, so unscored.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Jan 18 edition)
items.quote: This latter consensus has effectively erased expectations for near-term Fed action, with implied probabilities for the next few FOMC meetings now sitting at de minimis levels.
items.summary: El-Erian describes the DOJ subpoena of Powell and Powell's defiant video as an extraordinary escalation of the Trump-Fed feud, noting Treasury and dollar volatility stayed low. He says central bankers closed ranks around independence and Fed officials showed no urgency to cut, wiping out pricing of near-term moves.
items.score_note: Describes a hold for the next few FOMC meetings; no directional lean of his own.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs Exchanges podcast, recorded January 20 (published January 23)
items.quote: And the expectations are still for a cut or two in 2026.
items.summary: Solomon said the macro setup is pretty good for risk assets because of a confluence of stimulative policy: fiscal stimulus, monetary easing (100 basis points of cuts last year with a cut or two still expected in 2026), deregulation and an AI infrastructure investment boom. He expected more stimulative actions ahead of the midterms and saw geopolitics as the main uncertainty.
items.score_note: He cites the expectation of one or two more cuts in 2026 as part of his constructive base case; it is a description of expected easing, not a call for cuts, so -1.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box interview at World Economic Forum, Davos
items.quote: When you have conflicts, international geopolitical conflicts, even allies do not want to hold each other's debt.
items.summary: Dalio warns trade wars can turn into capital wars in which foreign holders are less willing to buy US debt while the US keeps issuing large volumes. He says the monetary order is breaking down and central banks prefer hard currency (gold) to fiat debt.
items.score_note: No view on the policy-rate path; about Treasury supply-demand and reserve diversification.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: Semafor interview at Davos
items.quote: You could easily imagine it could simply become unpopular to buy or hold US debt
items.summary: Dalio tells Semafor that US reliance on foreign buyers of its debt is an enormous vulnerability amid the Greenland dispute. He says it could become unpopular abroad to buy or hold US debt.
items.score_note: No policy-rate view; bond demand risk only.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: World Economic Forum, Davos, on-stage interview
items.quote: I don't like the courts doing stuff like that.
items.summary: At Davos Dimon criticised the administration's probe of Fed Chair Powell, saying courts should be very thoughtful before picking up something like that. Yahoo Finance's video page of the same session says (journalist's paraphrase, not a direct quote) that he called the probe lawfare but also argued the Fed is not quite as independent as people think. He also called the proposed 10% credit card rate cap an economic disaster.
items.score_note: Fed independence and the Powell probe only; no view on the rate path. The 'not as independent as people think' line was found only as a journalist's paraphrase.

items.speaker: Ken Griffin
items.occasion: Remarks at the World Economic Forum in Davos, reported by Reuters
items.quote: The easy money policies that Trump is trying to encourage the Fed to pursue increase the risk of inflation
items.summary: Griffin says Trump's tariffs raised US inflation and disrupted long-standing trade relationships, and that pushing the Fed toward easy money raises inflation risk and leaves Trump and his party politically exposed. Reuters notes he reiterated his concern about the administration's attacks on the Fed.
items.score_note: Pushes back on pressure for rate cuts on inflation grounds; does not call for hikes.

items.speaker: Larry Fink
items.occasion: World Economic Forum, Davos, panel discussion
items.quote: I think there will be big failures, but I don't think we are in a bubble,
items.summary: On a Davos panel Fink said the AI investment boom will produce big failures but is not a bubble, and that Western economies must scale spending to compete with China. He warned the build-out fails if the technology stays the domain of six hyperscalers. No comment on Fed policy.
items.score_note: AI capex view only; no rate-path content.
items.ai_quote: If technology is just the domain of the six hyperscalers, we will fail,

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: Fortune interview at World Economic Forum, Davos (with Kamal Ahmed)
items.quote: Do you print money or do you let a debt crisis happen?
items.summary: Dalio says the debt problem is so large that the monetary order is breaking down and policymakers face a choice between printing money and allowing a debt crisis. Fortune pairs this with his earlier remark that the debt will be repaid in devalued dollars.
items.score_note: He frames a dilemma (print vs. debt crisis) without saying which way the Fed will or should go in this quote. Debt-crisis remarks concern government debt, not private or corporate credit, so credit_view is null.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: Bloomberg interview at Goldman Sachs' annual Asia-Pacific conference
items.quote: I think the chance of a recession this year is low in the US
items.summary: Solomon put the base case for a US recession at one in seven and said he would not expect one without an exogenous event that changes sentiment. He expected a strong capital markets year with broader market participation, while noting the risk of a potential bubble in AI stocks and geopolitical speed bumps. No direct comment on the Fed in the reported remarks.
items.score_note: Growth and markets outlook only; the reference to the Fed's rate-cutting cycle in the article is the journalist's, not his.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Scott Wapner after the FOMC press conference (quotes via Business Insider)
items.quote: If you slash interest rates, then you're not only running a weaker dollar policy, but you're running an inflationary policy,
items.summary: Gundlach said inflation is running near 3% and that cutting rates below inflation would stoke prices and weaken the dollar further. He recommended non-US stocks, short-maturity bonds and precious metals, and said he was bearish on long bonds.
items.score_note: Warns against rate cuts as inflationary; no call for hikes, so +1.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Feb 1 edition)
items.quote: Warsh is a respected figure with deep expertise and experience, and a clear mandate to reform the central bank.
items.summary: After the January FOMC left rates unchanged and Trump nominated Kevin Warsh, El-Erian calls the Powell press conference uneventful and welcomes Warsh as a qualified reformer. He notes the confirmation timeline is uncertain because two senators are resisting until the DOJ probe of Powell is resolved.
items.score_note: Comments on the nominee and Fed reform, not on the direction of rates.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: Fireside chat with Ben Horowitz at an a16z founder event (held a few weeks before the a16z write-up of Feb 2)
items.quote: we’re in a rate cutting cycle
items.summary: In remarks quoted by a16z, Solomon listed fiscal stimulus, monetary stimulus, a rate cutting cycle and an AI capital investment supercycle as a cocktail of stimulus that makes it very hard to slow the economy down. He predicted 2026 could be the biggest M&A year in history.
items.score_note: Treats continued Fed easing as a given (rate cutting cycle); a forecast, not advocacy, so -1. The quote sits inside an ellipsized pull quote on the page; only the clause between the ellipses is used. Event date not stated; article date used.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Feb 7 edition)
items.quote: Second, what is the bond market’s appetite for funding this expansion, given widening spreads and some frisson in the leveraged loan market?
items.summary: El-Erian says softer labor data led markets to price a 60% chance of a June cut and that policy divergence among advanced-economy central banks could become a 2026 theme. On hyperscaler capex (Alphabet and Amazon alone guiding to about $400 billion) he asks whether the spending will pay off and whether the bond market will fund it given wider spreads and jitters in leveraged loans.
items.score_note: Reports market pricing of a June cut without endorsing it; main own view is the question about debt funding of AI capex.
items.ai_quote: Second, what is the bond market’s appetite for funding this expansion, given widening spreads and some frisson in the leveraged loan market?

items.speaker: Marc Rowan
items.occasion: Apollo Q4 2025 earnings call (Q&A)
items.quote: And so I do think that there is going to be increased dispersion amongst managers.
items.summary: Rowan says the market's reaction to software is extreme, with some quality companies down 50% to 70%, but stresses that direct-lending exposure is first lien and that Apollo's own software exposure is minimal. He expects more dispersion among managers after a long easy period.
items.score_note: Credit-quality commentary only; no view on the Fed or the rate path.
items.ai_quote: Most of the investments that are made into these private BDCs are de-risking for the individual making the investment.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: UBS Financial Services Conference, fireside chat
items.quote: There is uncertainty around inflation, and there's uncertainty on geopolitics.
items.summary: Solomon said 2026 could be a top-decile year for dealmaking, helped by deregulation and sponsors needing to return capital. He said the capital needed for the AI technology cycle will lift the overall capital-raising cycle and pointed to mega-cap tech firms raising debt for AI projects. He listed trade, inflation and geopolitics as uncertainties.
items.score_note: Mentions inflation only as an uncertainty; no view on the Fed rate path in the reported remarks.
items.ai_quote: The need for capital to continue on this technology cycle is going to have an impact on the overall capital-raising cycle

items.speaker: David Einhorn
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Sara Eisen
items.quote: I think by the time we get to the end of the year, it's going to be substantially more than two cuts
items.summary: Einhorn says there will be substantially more than the two cuts markets price and that Kevin Warsh will persuade the committee to cut by arguing productivity, even if the economy is running hot, unless inflation reaches 4% or 5%. He calls betting on more cuts one of the best trades available and says US fiscal and monetary policies 'don't make any sense', a reason he owns gold.
items.score_note: Explicit forecast of substantially more than two cuts in 2026.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: X post on wealth vs. money and bubbles (as quoted by Benzinga/Yahoo)
items.quote: And when there's a lot of wealth relative to the amount of hard money available — like we're seeing today — bubbles are created.
items.summary: Dalio posts that wealth is worth nothing unless it can be converted into money, and that today's high ratio of financial wealth to money creates bubbles. The article notes he compares the ratio to 1929 and 2000 and sees forced selling (e.g. for wealth taxes) as a possible popper.
items.score_note: No policy-rate view; bubble mechanics only.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: LinkedIn post on Blue Owl restricting withdrawals from a retail private-credit fund
items.quote: Is this a “canary-in-the-coalmine” moment, similar to August 2007?
items.summary: Reacting to Blue Owl permanently halting redemptions at a retail private-debt fund, El-Erian compares the episode to BNP Paribas freezing funds in August 2007. He says systemic risks are nowhere near 2008 scale but a significant valuation hit is looming for specific assets and private-market investing may have gone too far.
items.score_note: Credit-stress warning only; no statement on the Fed rate path.

items.speaker: Michael Burry
items.role: Investor, founder of Scion Asset Management
items.occasion: X post addressed to Oracle, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia and others, as embedded by Benzinga
items.quote: It is consuming all your cash flow, you are borrowing, you are financing in ways you never have
items.summary: Burry asks the hyperscalers when spending on the AI data-center buildout actually ends, saying it consumes all their cash flow and forces borrowing and unfamiliar financing. He accuses them of accounting tricks that hide expense by stretching depreciation and says asset quality matters in the long run.
items.score_note: AI capex financing and accounting critique; no monetary-policy content.
items.ai_quote: It is consuming all your cash flow, you are borrowing, you are financing in ways you never have

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Feb 22 edition)
items.quote: this does not appear to be a systemic risk on par with what led to the Global Financial Crisis
items.summary: El-Erian notes core PCE came in hot at 3.0% and that the Fed minutes showed a widening range of views, with several participants wanting language that keeps rate hikes possible. On private credit he says investing has reached excessive levels and 'market-for-lemons' effects should be expected, but he does not see GFC-scale systemic risk.
items.score_note: Reports the two-sided tone of the Fed minutes without taking a rate view; main message is that private-credit stress is real but not systemic.
items.ai_quote: private credit investing has reached excessive levels in advanced economies

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: JPMorgan Chase 2026 Company Update (investor day), Q&A
items.quote: I think that the balance sheet of the Fed is too big.
items.summary: Dimon says the Fed's balance sheet is too big, that it has lost $1 trillion and took its eye off interest-rate exposure, and that it cannot shrink the balance sheet without changing LCR and liquidity rules; he expects Warsh's review to take about a year and not to be done too quickly. On credit he says today's competition resembles 2005 to 2007, with a rising tide lifting all boats and 'a couple of people doing some dumb things', and that the credit cycle will turn with surprises.
items.score_note: View is on the size of the Fed balance sheet and bank liquidity rules, not on the policy-rate path; left unscored.

items.speaker: Howard Marks
items.occasion: Oaktree memo 'AI Hurtles Ahead'
items.quote: no one should go all-in without acknowledging that they face the risk of ruin if things go badly
items.summary: Follow-up to his December 'Is It a Bubble?' memo. Marks says AI is real and its potential more likely underestimated, but infrastructure booms always cause capital to be malinvested, some AI revenue is circular, and none of that says AI assets are fairly priced. He advises a moderate, selective position. No comment on Fed policy.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content; AI-investment bubble discussion only. credit_view bubble_warning is a mild one (he advises neither all-in nor all-out).
items.ai_quote: Claude’s answer doesn’t necessarily preclude the possibility that demand growth could slow or infrastructure building could run ahead of it.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Project Syndicate op-ed 'What Will the Fed’s “Warsh Era” Bring?'
items.quote: To focus solely on rate cuts is to misunderstand the Fed’s situation and the scale of the challenge awaiting its next leader.
items.summary: El-Erian argues that speculation about how hard Warsh will push for rate cuts misses the point. He says the next chair inherits a Fed that is fractured internally and lacks credibility externally, and that Warsh should strengthen its analytical framework and establish a balance-sheet theory.
items.score_note: Explicitly sets the rate question aside in favor of institutional and balance-sheet reform.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: LinkedIn post on the drivers of market risk aversion
items.quote: Additional red flags in the private credit markets in advanced countries, including news about loose underwriting standards, write-downs, and fraud.
items.summary: El-Erian lists reasons for the risk aversion that pushed stocks down and the 10-year Treasury yield below 4%: geopolitical tensions, unemployment worries after Block said it would cut 40% of its workforce, and more red flags in private credit such as loose underwriting, write-downs and fraud.
items.score_note: Market and credit commentary; no view on the Fed rate path.
items.ai_quote: Additional red flags in the private credit markets in advanced countries, including news about loose underwriting standards, write-downs, and fraud.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Mar 1 edition, after the US-Israel strikes on Iran)
items.quote: Also, as energy costs rise and growth faces more headwinds, the path for central banks becomes even trickier.
items.summary: Writing after the weekend US-Israel military action against Iran, El-Erian says the cumulative disruptions raise the prospect of a fresh bout of stagflation in a so-far resilient global economy. He says higher energy costs and weaker growth make the central-bank path trickier.
items.score_note: Stagflation framing with two-sided risks for central banks; no directional call.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview at JPMorgan's leveraged finance conference, Miami Beach
items.quote: It’s been coming down, but it seems to maybe have leveled off around 3%.
items.summary: Two days after the US and Israel struck Iran, Dimon called inflation the skunk at the party and said it seems to have leveled off around 3%. He said the conflict would add only a teeny bit to inflation and would not be a major inflationary hit unless prolonged. He also said asset prices are high and there is more exuberance than there should be.
items.score_note: No explicit Fed call. Inflation is his main risk (stuck near 3%) but he played down the Iran shock unless prolonged; torn between 0 and +1, chose the level nearer 0.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: Australian Financial Review Business Summit, Sydney (Tuesday March 3 local time)
items.quote: I think the market reaction has been more benign, given the magnitude of this, than you might think.
items.summary: Days into the Iran war Solomon said he was surprised by how benign the market reaction had been and that markets would need a couple of weeks to digest it. He said the things to watch are whether it becomes prolonged, filters into energy supply chains and affects consumer sentiment. Bloomberg reported he also said he is watching private credit portfolios for frothiness (not verified, paywalled).
items.score_note: Energy-shock and market commentary only; no statement on what the Fed should or will do.

items.speaker: Marc Rowan
items.occasion: Interview at Bloomberg Invest, New York, as reported by Investing.com
items.quote: This will be a shakeout — I don't think it is going to be short term
items.summary: Rowan warns that a shakeout is coming for private-credit firms amid concerns about defaults on loans to software companies and redemptions at business development companies. He calls it foreseeable and says all a manager can do is to have been a good underwriter and risk manager.
items.score_note: Private-credit stress view only; nothing on the rate path.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: All-In Podcast interview with David Friedberg (published Mar 3; transcript copy)
items.quote: But you can’t make interest rates severely artificially low because one man’s debts are another man’s assets.
items.summary: Dalio says the Fed faces a hard balancing act: rates too low hurt creditors and fuel a bubble, rates too high squeeze debtors, and a K-shaped economy makes one rate fit badly. He thinks re-expansion of the Fed balance sheet is likely down the road, calls Warsh a practical man with a tough job, and says AI is eating everything and might eat itself by not producing adequate profits.
items.score_note: On rates he argues for balance (not artificially low, not too high) = 0; separately he forecasts Fed Treasury buying is 'likely down the road', which leans -1 on the balance sheet.
items.ai_quote: Right now it looks to me like AI basically is eating everything and it might eat itself.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: LinkedIn post on a Bloomberg headline about private-credit funds capping withdrawals
items.quote: It’s a classic contagion phenomenon: "If you can’t sell what you want, you sell what you can."
items.summary: Reacting to a Bloomberg headline on private credit (Business Insider identifies it as Morgan Stanley and Cliffwater capping fund withdrawals), El-Erian warns of an 'ATM' scenario in which investors liquidate healthy funds because they are the available source of cash. He says the line between liquidity and solvency can blur under extreme conditions, adding 'we are not at that point' but it is worth watching.
items.score_note: Contagion warning on private-credit liquidity; no rate-path view.

items.speaker: Larry Fink
items.occasion: BlackRock 2026 Infrastructure Summit, panel discussion (held the week of the article)
items.quote: They may in the short run overinvest, but the long-term demand will catch up,
items.summary: Fink said one or two bankruptcies among AI players are inevitable and that this is capitalism. He wants more, not less, AI infrastructure investment and said hyperscalers may overinvest in the short run but demand will catch up. He was not worried about their debt-funded spending, noting their return on equity is still better than BlackRock's.
items.score_note: AI capex and hyperscaler financing only; no rate-path content.

items.summary: El-Erian raises his US recession odds from about 25% to 35% because of the oil shock from the Iran war. He describes a two-phase bear case of higher inflation followed by lower growth and higher unemployment, and warns that hotter inflation could interact with fragilities such as private-credit redemptions and trigger a financial accident that tightens credit.
items.score_note: Stagflation and financial-accident risk; he does not say what the Fed will or should do.

coverage_notes: Window 2026-01-01 to 2026-05-31. Every quote and ai_quote was re-checked by substring match against its page, both with a browser-style fetch and with the same curl method pipeline.py uses (89 of 89 exact on 2026-11-23). Method: firms' own pages first (Oaktree memos, JPMorgan letter and official call transcripts, BlackRock letter, Goldman and Morgan Stanley shareholder letters), Motley Fool transcript pages for BlackRock, Goldman, Morgan Stanley and Apollo calls, then news articles with direct quotes found mostly through StockNow news search (Yahoo Finance, CNBC, Fortune, Business Insider) and El-Erian's own LinkedIn posts. Gaps: David Tepper, no on-topic statement found in the window (0 items). Paul Tudor Jones, only the Apr 28 podcast and the May 7 CNBC interview; no CNBC full-transcript page found and nothing for January to March. Howard Marks, the two memos only; a Mar 17 fireside chat and a May 5 podcast are in unverified. Bill Ackman, January only. Ken Griffin, Davos Jan 21 and Milken May 5 only. Ted Pick, Davos and Apr 15 Bloomberg interviews are video-only. Gundlach's Mar 10, Mar 18 (FOMC day) and Mar 26 appearances have no open direct quote. El-Erian weekly notes for Jan 25, Apr 26, May 3, May 24 and May 31 were not located. Steve Cohen, nothing found. Earnings calls: JPMorgan Jan 13 call had no Fed or credit-cycle remarks by Dimon (his Fed-independence remarks that day were on the media call, which is itemized); Goldman Jan 15 call had only a passing mention of monetary stimulus and is not itemized; no open transcript page was found for the BlackRock Jan 15 call (Fink's CNBC interview that day is itemized instead). Scoring: 57 of 89 items are unscored because they address only credit stress, AI financing or Fed independence. Judgment calls to review: Gundlach Mar 23 (+1 rests on DoubleLine's recap, the quote is about credit), Gundlach Jan 13 (0 from a paraphrase), Dimon Apr 28 (+1 leans on Fortune's report of the same event), Ackman Jan 11 (+1 for fewer cuts than priced, although he also expects the Fed to drop the 2% goal), Dalio Jan 8 and May 7 (set to null by the lead collector: long-run debt-monetization thesis, not a rate-path call). Private-credit warnings tied to AI disruption of software loans are tagged ai_financing. Where score is null and the sub-collector left score_basis empty it was filled with 'forecast' as a placeholder.
